h1: The 8 Best Printers for Envelopes of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Printers for Envelopes: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: the 8 best printers for envelopes, comparing laser and inkjet models on tray design, duplex, and everyday mailing use.
summary: The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the best printer for envelopes: laser toner that resists smearing, plus copy and scan in a compact body. The HL-L2405W does the same print job for less, and the Canon LBP6030w is the cheapest laser here. Choose the HL-L3220CDW when logos in color matter. The inkjets suit occasional mail only.
intro: An envelope is the hardest thing most home printers ever touch. It is thicker than copy paper, it has a folded seam and a glued flap, and it must travel a straighter path than a flat sheet. Cheap machines answer with jams, creased corners and smeared return addresses, and the first stack of stamps-ready envelopes goes in the bin.

So this ranking leans on mechanism over marketing. We reviewed eight printers by spec sheet and scored each on the Primea framework, with engine type weighted first because heat-fused toner resists smearing and moisture better than water-based ink. Feed design, duplex, extra functions and price tier came next. No spec sheet promises flawless results on every envelope size, so we treat feed design as the deciding hardware feature.

products.name: Brother DCP-L2640DW Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser
products.verdict: A compact laser all-in-one built for steady mailing.
products.description:
The DCP-L2640DW is a compact monochrome laser with automatic duplex, copy, scan and wireless and mobile printing. For envelopes the engine is the argument: laser toner is fused to the surface with heat, so a return address stays sharp and does not bleed if the envelope picks up a little moisture in the mailbag.

It tops the list ahead of the HL-L2405W because it keeps every laser benefit and adds a scanner and copier, so one machine handles invoices, forms and mailing. It also costs the most of the lasers here, at the $200 to $500 tier.

Buy it if you mail regularly and want a single device for the office. The caveat is color: addresses print in black only, so branded stationery needs the HL-L3220CDW instead.
products.skipIf: You need color on the envelope.

products.name: Brother HL-L2405W Wireless Compact Monochrome Laser
products.verdict: A print-only laser with low per-page toner cost.
products.description:
Brother's HL-L2405W is the pure envelope machine, print-only and monochrome, with wireless and mobile printing and a low per-page toner cost, in the $100 to $200 tier. Because toner cost is the recurring expense of mail merges, that spec matters more here than speed.

It ranks second because it gives up the DCP-L2640DW's scanner, copier and duplex, then passes the saving to you. If envelopes and letters are all you print, those three missing features cost you nothing. Against the Canon LBP6030w below, the extra spend buys mobile printing the Canon does not list.

Buy it for a home office that mails often and prints little else. The honest limit is no scanner, so every signed page that must go back digitally needs a phone app or another device.
products.idealFor: Home offices printing envelopes on a budget.
products.skipIf: You need scanning or two-sided printing.

products.name: Brother HL-L3220CDW Wireless Color Laser Printer
products.verdict: Color laser output for branded envelopes, up to 19 PPM.
products.description:
The HL-L3220CDW brings color laser to envelopes. It lists up to 19 PPM, a 250-sheet tray, automatic duplex, and wireless and mobile compatibility, in the $200 to $500 tier, and it is built for daily office use.

It sits third because most envelope jobs are black text, and color toner multiplies running cost across four cartridges. What you get in return is a logo or a colored return address that survives handling, which inkjet ink cannot promise. For shops sending branded mailings, it is the clear winner over the monochrome Brothers.

Buy it if presentation counts: wedding suites, boutique orders, client mailers. Skip it if you only print black addresses, because the toner expense shows up on every cartridge change.
products.skipIf: Black text is all you print.

products.name: Canon imageCLASS LBP6030w Monochrome Wireless Laser Printer
products.verdict: The least expensive laser here, at 19 PPM.
products.description:
Canon's LBP6030w is the cheapest way into laser here, a print-only monochrome unit running 19 PPM with a compact wireless design and a 1-year limited warranty, in the $50 to $100 tier. Toner fusing is what separates it from every inkjet below it.

It lands fourth because its shortcuts show next to the Brothers. The listing carries no mobile printing feature, there is no duplex, and the design is plainly older. Spend the extra to reach the HL-L2405W and you pick up mobile support and a lower stated per-page toner cost.

Buy it if you want smear-resistant addresses on the smallest budget and print from a desktop. Skip it if your phone is how you print, since the listing never mentions that capability and you would be relying on a workaround.
products.skipIf: You need scanning or mobile printing.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TR4720 All-in-One Wireless Printer
products.verdict: An inkjet with a single envelope feed and an ADF.
products.description:
The PIXMA TR4720 brings an auto document feeder, built-in fax, mobile printing and a tray that accepts a single envelope at a time. It sits in the $50 to $100 tier.

Single-envelope feeding is the limit. You hand-load each piece, so a batch of 40 invitations turns into a chore, and inkjet ink can smear on glossy or damp stock. That is why every laser here outranks it. It does lead the other inkjets because the feeder and fax make it useful for general office work between mailings.

Buy it if envelopes are a sideline and you also scan or fax paper. Skip it if you mail in volume, where the hand-feed and smear risk both add up.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS4320 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: A duplex inkjet that suits occasional card and invitation envelopes.
products.description:
The TS4320 prints in color on both sides, copies and scans, and lists envelope support at the tray, all in a compact footprint. It sits in the $50 to $100 tier and puts color at the center of the pitch.

That color is why it suits holiday cards, wedding invitations and party mailers, where a printed pattern or a colored name matters more than speed. It ranks below the TR4720 for business use because it lacks a document feeder, which makes multi-page scanning slower.

Buy it for personal mailing a few times a year. Skip it if you post daily, since inkjet ink can smear on some envelopes and the ink will cost more per page than toner. If you test a new envelope stock, run a single sheet first and let it dry before stacking.

products.name: HP DeskJet 4355 Wireless All-in-One Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: Guided envelope alignment with a 3-month Instant Ink trial.
products.description:
HP's DeskJet 4355 pairs a small-footprint color inkjet body with a tray envelope feed, AI-capable printing features and a 3-month Instant Ink trial. The software angle is its distinction: guided alignment in the app is meant to cut the wasted envelopes that come from loading them the wrong way.

It ranks seventh because the spec sheet adds software, not hardware. The Canons above it add a feeder or duplex, and none of them depends on an app to feed paper correctly. The Instant Ink trial also lasts only three months, so judge the ongoing ink cost before enrolling.

Buy it if you are new to envelope printing and want step-by-step help. Skip it if you mail in volume, because the feed is limited and inkjet ink adds up.

products.name: Canon PIXMA TS6520 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer
products.verdict: An OLED display walks you through envelope setup.
products.description:
Canon's TS6520 mounts a 1.42-inch OLED display on a color inkjet that prints two-sided, copies and scans. The screen is the feature: instead of guessing at menu settings, you read prompts at the printer itself.

It ranks last because nothing else in the listing speaks to envelopes. There is no envelope-specific feature beyond the general tray, and ink can smear on some stock, which puts it behind both the lasers and the TS4320 that shares its duplex and copy hardware. The OLED guidance helps the first time you load an envelope and then fades into the background.

Buy it if you want on-screen prompts and print envelopes only now and then. Skip it if you want a laser, or if the mailing work is steady.

whatMatters.detail: Laser toner is heat-fused to the page, so it resists smearing and moisture. Inkjet ink is water-based and can bleed on glossy or damp envelopes. That difference is why the Brother DCP-L2640DW and HL-L2405W outrank every inkjet here. Confirm the engine type in the product title before you read any other spec on the page.

Some printers feed envelopes one at a time through a rear slot, while others pull from a stack. A single feed is slow for volume, as on the Canon PIXMA TR4720, and every hand-loaded piece is another chance to skew it. Look for envelope feed notes in the bullets, and see what the manual says about stack capacity.

Duplex prints both sides automatically. It helps for letters and invoices but is rarely needed for the envelope itself. It matters if the same printer produces your documents, since flipping pages by hand wastes time. The Brother DCP-L2640DW and HL-L3220CDW list it, while the HL-L2405W does not. Check the spec table before ordering.

Toner usually costs less per page than ink at volume, and the Brother HL-L2405W lists a low per-page toner cost. Color lasers like the HL-L3220CDW multiply that by four cartridges. If you mail often, running cost beats sticker price within a year. Look for yield or cost per page in the listing, or on the cartridge page.

Standard business envelopes feed easily on most printers, but large, padded or square sizes may not. The envelope path is narrower than the paper path, and an unsupported size can crease or jam. Check the supported sizes in the printer manual before you buy, and test the printer on one envelope before running a full stack.

faq.a: Not all. Check the listing for envelope support or a dedicated feed. The Canon PIXMA TR4720 takes a single envelope at a time, while the Brother lasers suit steady mailing because they take a stack and fuse toner that will not smear in transit.

Feeding envelopes without choosing the envelope setting, which causes jams and smears. Pick the envelope size in the print dialog first, then load as the manual shows. The Brother HL-L2405W and Canon LBP6030w both reward this step.

faq.q: Is laser worth it over inkjet?
faq.a: For regular mailing, yes. Toner from the Brother DCP-L2640DW resists smearing and moisture, while inkjet ink on the TS4320 or TS6520 can bleed. For a few invitations a year, an inkjet is acceptable, as long as you let the ink dry before stacking.

faq.q: How do I set up envelope printing?
faq.a: Select the envelope size in the print dialog, then load the envelope in the orientation the manual shows. The HP DeskJet 4355 adds guided alignment in its app, and the Canon TS6520 shows prompts on its OLED screen.

Use flat envelopes without bubbles or lumps, and on a single-feed model like the PIXMA TR4720 load one at a time. Avoid stacking freshly printed inkjet envelopes while the ink is wet, since that causes smears.

faq.q: Can I print on large envelopes?
faq.a: Check the supported sizes in the manual before buying, since envelope paths are narrower than paper paths. Standard business envelopes are common, but large or padded ones may not feed on compact models such as the Canon LBP6030w or Brother HL-L2405W.

finalTake: For envelopes, buy a laser. The Brother DCP-L2640DW is the best printer here, thanks to smear-resistant toner and a scanner and copier for the rest of the office. If you only print mail, the HL-L2405W saves money, and the Canon LBP6030w is the cheapest laser. Choose the HL-L3220CDW for color branding. Keep the inkjets for occasional cards, not steady mailing.
